newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Air NZ says tough to match 1996 profit in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Air NZ says tough to match 1996 profit in 1997.

text.p: Air New Zealand Ltd said on Monday it expected "intensive competition" to continue in both the Australian domestic and international air transport markets.
"Against this background, the directors presently expect that it will prove difficult to maintain 1997 earnings at, or above, the 1996 outcome," the airline said.
Air NZ said its June 1996 year net profit of $225.2 million, while 13.4 percent below the 1995 result, was still the group's second best profit.
The directors said the result was creditable in view of the more difficult trading conditions which prevailed in the second half.
While international passenger revenues increased by 3.3 percent, the stronger New Zealand dollar reduced receipts from overseas sales in foreign currencies by around $100 million.
Growth in total passenger traffic to New Zealand was below that anticipated at the beginning of the year.

Visitor arrival growth fell from 10.7 percent for the 1995 year to 7.6 percent reflecting local conditions in key offshore markets such at the U.S., Japan and Germany, and strong competition from other tourist destinations around the world.

New Zealanders took 16.8 percent more short term trips overseas in the 12 months to June 1996, largely reflecting the heavily discounted fares available on the Tasman and a stronger New Zealand currency.
Australia continued to be the most popular destination for New Zealand travellers, accounting for 52.1 percent of outbound traffic during the 1996 year.

Competition from other international operators intensified, particularly during the second half of the year when fare discounting became more prevalent as airlines sought to use the increased capacity committed to routes to and from Australasia.

Less significant, but noteworthy, were the adverse effects on both domestic and international airline operations of industrial action taken by air traffic controllers against their employer, the Airways Corporation, and the ongoing volcanic eruptions at Mount Ruapehu which were particularly disruptive for domestic services.
A steady final dividend of 12 cents per share maintained the total dividend at 20 cents.
